Think about reproduction - how many offspring do most organisms produce compared with the number needed just to replace the parents?
If so many are born but population size stays roughly constant, what must be happening to most individuals, and why do they have to struggle with each other and the environment?
Remember no two members of a species look exactly alike - where does that inbuilt phenotypic difference come from at the DNA level?
Link that struggle to the environment - what name do we give to factors like predators, disease, food shortage and climate that decide who survives?

walkthrough:
The Big Idea of Evolution**
All living things share a simple pattern. Populations of organisms change over time. That gradual change in inherited characteristics is evolution itself, and natural selection is the mechanism that drives it.

Overproduction and the Struggle**
Most species produce far more offspring than are needed to keep numbers stable. Since resources like food, mates and shelter are limited, population size stays roughly constant. That means many individuals must die, so individuals compete for survival. We call the environmental challenges that kill or hold back some individuals selection pressures.

Where Variation Comes From**
Competition would mean nothing if everyone was identical. Within a species there is always variation in phenotype, and that is underpinned by genetic variation. New alleles arise originally by mutation, so some individuals happen to carry combinations that work slightly better in the current environment.

Differential Survival and Inheritance**
This is survival of the fittest in the Darwinian sense - fittest means best adapted to that environment, not strongest. Individuals with advantageous alleles have a selective advantage, so they are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass those advantageous alleles to their offspring, while disadvantageous alleles are lost.

From Selection to Evolution**
Because successful alleles are passed on more often, their frequency in the gene pool increases generation after generation. Over long periods this directional change in allele frequency alters the whole population and can eventually lead to speciation.

Final answer: General theory: organisms change over time. Organisms produce many offspring, more than needed to maintain the population, but population size remains constant. Within a species there is phenotypic variation due to genetic variation caused by mutation. Individuals compete for survival / survival of the fittest under selection pressures. Better adapted individuals with advantageous alleles / selective advantage survive, pass on advantageous alleles to offspring, changing allele frequency, which can lead to speciation.

hints: Split the story into two halves - what shuffles alleles when gametes are made, and what shuffles them again when gametes join?
Picture prophase I - homologous chromosomes pair as bivalents, so what could happen if chromatids touch and swap pieces?
Be precise about which chromatids swap - sister or non-sister - and what exactly is exchanged between them.
Think about genes that are normally inherited together on the same chromosome - how would swapping pieces affect those linkage groups?
Now move to metaphase I - the bivalents line up on the equator, but which parent's chromosome faces which pole?
Extend the same random lining-up idea to the second division of meiosis and to the possibility of errors in chromosome number or structure.
Leave meiosis and think about mating - do organisms choose mates and gametes in a fixed, identical way every time?
Finally, think about fertilisation itself - out of millions of genetically different sperm and eggs, which two actually fuse?
walkthrough:
Crossing Over Creates New Chromosomes**
In prophase I homologous chromosomes pair up to form a bivalent. Non-sister chromatids - one from the maternal homologue and one from the paternal homologue - form chiasmata and cross over. They break and exchange sections of DNA / genetic material.

Why Crossing Over Matters**
Genes on the same chromosome are normally linked and travel together as a linkage group. Crossing over breaks those linkage groups and puts maternal and paternal alleles onto the same chromatid. Every recombinant chromatid therefore carries a new combination of alleles that neither parent chromosome had.

Independent Assortment Shuffles Whole Chromosomes**
At metaphase I, bivalents line up randomly at the equator - for each pair it is chance whether the maternal or paternal homologue faces a given pole. At metaphase II, sister chromatids / chromosomes also assort randomly. With 23 pairs in humans this random assortment alone can generate over 8 million different chromosome combinations in gametes. Occasional chromosome mutation during meiosis adds further variation.

Fertilisation Shuffles Gametes**
Variation does not stop at meiosis. Random mating means any male can mate with any female, and fertilisation involves random fusion of gametes. Each sperm and each egg is already genetically different, so which two fuse is pure chance, producing a unique diploid zygote every time.

Final answer: Meiosis: in prophase I, chiasmata / crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes / bivalent, exchanging DNA / genetic material, breaking linkage groups to give new combinations of alleles. Random / independent assortment of homologous chromosomes / bivalents at metaphase I and of sister chromatids / chromosomes at metaphase II gives different chromosome combinations. Possible chromosome mutation adds variation. Fertilisation: random mating and random fusion / fertilisation of genetically different gametes produces unique diploid zygotes.
